01.note: Rava created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira spoke to him, but the man did not answer. Rabbi Zeira said to him: You were made by one of the Sages; return to your dust.
01.why: Rava has just taught that the righteous could create a world if they wished; the Gemara tells of his created man as evidence for that claim, and follows it with another such report.

people.about: A Sage who, according to the story, created a man

people.about: The Sage to whom Rava sent his creation; he sends it back to dust

terms.meaning: The translation's word for Rava's created man: a human figure made by a Sage, which here can move but cannot speak.

02.note: Rav told Rabbi Hiyya that he had seen an Arab slice a camel with a sword, beat a drum, and the camel stood up again. Rabbi Hiyya asked whether there had been blood and excrement on the ground afterward. Since there had not, he concluded it was only a trick on the eyes, not real sorcery.
02.why: The discussion is about what magicians and demons can and cannot really do; Rabbi Hiyya's question shows how to tell a mere illusion from real sorcery, a distinction the mishna under discussion uses to decide who is liable.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who reports what he saw an Arab do to a camel

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage Rav tells; he shows it was an illusion

terms.meaning: An illusion that only makes it look as if something happened, as opposed to real sorcery that actually changes things.

03.note: Ze'eiri came to Alexandria in Egypt and bought a donkey. When he went to give it water, the spell broke and the donkey turned into the plank of a bridge. The sellers refunded his money, telling him they would not have done so for anyone but Ze'eiri, since everyone there tests a purchase with water before buying.
03.why: It is one of a string of tales about sorcery and illusion told while the Gemara discusses what magicians can really do.

people.name: Ze'eiri
people.about: A Sage who bought a bewitched donkey in Alexandria; the sellers refund him because of who he is

04.note: Yannai came to an inn and asked for water. He was brought a drink of flour and water, and he saw the innkeeper woman's lips moving. He spilled a little of it and it turned into scorpions. He said: I drank from yours, now you drink from mine. He gave her a drink and she turned into a donkey; he rode her to the marketplace. Her friend came and broke the spell, and people saw him riding on a woman in the marketplace.
04.why: It is one of a string of sorcery tales the Gemara tells while discussing what magicians can and cannot really do.

people.about: A man who uncovered a spell on his drink and turned the innkeeper woman into a donkey

people.about: She put a spell on Yannai's drink and was turned into a donkey

05.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues came to visit. It was Friday, and when his son Hyrcanus came to remove his phylacteries, Rabbi Eliezer scolded him for neglecting the serious Sabbath preparations. Seeing his mind was clear, the Sages sat four cubits away from him. He rebuked them for not coming to learn sooner, predicted they would not die a natural death and Rabbi Akiva's would be worse, and mourned the Torah dying with him, including the magic of planting cucumbers that only Akiva had asked him about. He answered their questions on ritual purity and died saying the word pure. Rabbi Yehoshua declared his ban lifted. After the Sabbath, Rabbi Akiva met the funeral, beat his flesh until it bled, and cried: I have many coins and no money changer.
05.why: The mishna says Rabbi Akiva learned about magically gathering cucumbers from Rabbi Yehoshua; the Gemara asks how, since this account shows he learned it from Rabbi Eliezer. It answers that he learned it from Eliezer but understood it only from Yehoshua.

06.note: On his deathbed, Rabbi Eliezer recalls a walk with his student Akiva. Akiva asked him to teach him about planting cucumbers. Rabbi Eliezer said one statement, and the whole field filled with cucumbers. Akiva asked to be taught how to uproot them; Rabbi Eliezer said one statement, and they all gathered into one place.
06.why: The mishna mentions gathering cucumbers by sorcery as Rabbi Akiva's teaching; this memory shows where Akiva first learned it, and the Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Eliezer was allowed to perform magic at all.

07.note: Burglars broke into Rava's house and stole his rams. Later they came to return them, but Rava refused to take them back, saying: Since this ruling came from Rav's mouth.
07.why: The Gemara is discussing Rav's ruling that a burglar who could lawfully be killed takes ownership of what he stole; Rava's refusal shows that he acted on Rav's ruling himself.

people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling Rava cites

terms.meaning: Thieves who tunnel or break into a house; the Torah allows the homeowner to kill such a burglar, which affects whether the burglar must return what he took.

08.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that a man set his eyes on a woman and became so lovesick he was near death. Doctors said he would be cured only if she slept with him. The Sages said: Let him die rather than that. The doctors asked that she at least stand naked before him, then that she at least talk with him behind a fence. Each time the Sages said: Let him die.
08.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a person must die rather than transgress, including forbidden sexual relations; this case extends that to even small acts of intimacy, and the Gemara then debates whether the woman was married.

09.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avuya taught that the skull of King Jehoiakim bore the words: This and yet another. The grandfather of Rabbi Perida found a skull lying at the gates of Jerusalem with those words on it. He buried it twice and twice it came back up, so he knew it was Jehoiakim's. Saying a king should not be disgraced, he wrapped it in silk and put it in a chest. His wife found it, and the neighbors told her it must be the skull of his first wife whom he could not forget. She heated the oven and burned it. When he came home he said: This is what was written on it, This and yet another.
09.why: It follows another teaching of Rabbi Hiyya bar Avuya in the discussion about relations with gentile women; the Gemara gathers a second saying of his and the story that bears it out.

10.note: The Roman emperor challenged Rabban Gamliel: You say the dead will live, but they become dust, and can dust come to life? The emperor's daughter said: Leave him, I will answer him. She asked her father which of two craftsmen is greater, one who shapes vessels from water or one who shapes them from clay. He said the one who works with water. She answered: If he can shape from water, surely he can shape from clay.
10.why: The discussion is gathering arguments for the resurrection of the dead; the daughter's parable joins Rabbi Meir's answer to Cleopatra and the reasoning from glass vessels that follows.

11.note: The people of Afrikiya came before Alexander of Macedon claiming the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls it the land of Canaan and Canaan was their ancestor. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages for permission to argue: if he lost, they could say only a simple man had lost; if he won, the Torah of Moses had won. He cited the Torah's curse that Canaan would be a slave to his brothers: a slave's property belongs to his master, and they owed years of unpaid service besides. Alexander told them to answer. They asked for three days, found no answer, and fled, leaving their fields sown and vineyards planted. It was a Sabbatical Year.
11.why: The Gemara has just told of Geviha ben Pesisa's sharp reply to a heretic about resurrection; it now brings his debates on behalf of the Jewish people, recorded as the reason for a holiday on the 24th of Nisan.

12.note: The Egyptians came before Alexander of Macedon demanding back the silver and gold the Israelites had borrowed when they left Egypt. Geviha ben Pesisa got the Sages' permission to argue the case. He cited the Torah's verse that Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years and demanded wages for 600,000 people enslaved all that time. Alexander told the Egyptians to answer; they asked for three days, found no answer, and fled, leaving their fields sown and vineyards planted. It was a Sabbatical Year.
12.why: It is the second of three debates in which Geviha ben Pesisa defends the Jewish people before Alexander, told after his reply to a heretic about resurrection.

13.note: The descendants of Ishmael and of Keturah came before Alexander of Macedon claiming a share of the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls both Ishmael and Isaac sons of Abraham. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages for permission to argue against them: if he lost, they could say only a simple man had lost; if he won, the Torah of Moses had won. They gave him permission and he went. His argument and the outcome are not given here.
13.why: It is the third of Geviha ben Pesisa's debates for the Jewish people before Alexander.

14.note: Bar Koziva ruled for two and a half years and told the Sages: I am the Messiah. They answered that the Messiah is said to judge by smell, and they would see whether he could. When they saw he could not, they killed him.
14.why: Rava has just read Isaiah's verse to mean the Messiah will judge by smell; the story puts that test to a man who claimed to be the Messiah.

15.note: Rava used to think there was no truth anywhere in the world, until Rav Tavut, a Sage who would not lie for all the world's wealth, told him this. He once came to a place called Truth, where no one lied and no one died before their time. He married a woman there and had two sons. One day his wife was washing her hair when a neighbor knocked; thinking it improper to say she was bathing, he said she was not there. His two sons died. The townspeople asked what had happened, and when he told them, they begged him to leave so he would not bring early death upon them.
15.why: A teaching has just said that before the Messiah comes truth will be lacking; this story, about the one place where truth lived, is told on that theme.

16.note: Rav Hanan bar Tahlifa sent word to Rav Yosef that he had met a man holding a scroll in Hebrew script and language. The man said he had served as a hired soldier in the Roman army and found it in the Roman archives. The scroll said that 4,291 years after creation the world would end, with the wars of the sea monsters, the wars of Gog and Magog, and the days of the Messiah, and that God would renew the world only after seven thousand years. Rav Aha, son of Rava, said the text read five thousand.
16.why: The Gemara is weighing traditions about when the Messiah will come; this scroll gives a date, and the discussion goes on to warn against calculating the end.

17.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi found Elijah the prophet at the entrance to Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's tomb and asked if he would reach the World-to-Come; Elijah answered, If this Master wishes. He asked when the Messiah would come; Elijah told him to go ask him, at the gate of Rome, sitting among the sick poor, unbinding and rebinding one bandage at a time so he will be ready. Rabbi Yehoshua greeted him, and the Messiah greeted him back and said he would come today. When he did not come, Rabbi Yehoshua told Elijah the Messiah had lied. Elijah said he had meant: today, if you will listen to his voice.
17.why: The Gemara has been reading verses that say the redemption can come early if Israel merits it; the Messiah's 'today, if you listen' makes the same point in a story.

18.note: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's students asked when the Messiah would come. He hesitated, fearing they would ask for a sign; they promised not to. He said: when this gate falls and is rebuilt, falls and is rebuilt, and falls again, and before it can be rebuilt the son of David will come. They then asked for a sign anyway, and he said the water of the Cave of Pamyas would turn to blood, and it did. As he was dying he told them to bury his coffin deep, because every palm tree in Babylonia would have a Persian horse tied to it and every coffin in the Land of Israel would become a feed trough for Median horses.
18.why: It is one of several teachings about the signs and timing of the Messiah's coming in this part of the discussion.

19.note: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were mending the cloth covers for the scrolls in Rav Yehuda's school. When they came to the scroll of Esther, they said this one does not need a cover. Rav Yehuda told them that talking this way also looks like irreverence.
19.why: The mishna lists the epikoros among those who lose the World-to-Come, and the Gemara is collecting examples of what counts as such disrespect; this remark about the scroll of Esther is one.

20.note: A student had mocked Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that God would set gates of giant jewels in Jerusalem. Later the student's ship set sail and he saw angels cutting precious stones; they said God would set them in Jerusalem's gates. Back home he told Rabbi Yohanan: Teach, master, it suits you; just as you said, so I saw. Rabbi Yohanan said: Good-for-nothing, had you not seen, you would not have believed? You mock the words of the Sages. He set his eyes on him and turned him into a pile of bones.
20.why: Rabbi Zeira cites this case to show when agreeing with a Sage is irreverent: the student agreed only after seeing, which proved he had mocked. The discussion is about what makes a person an epikoros.
